On four datasets covering the brain (CC359), knee (fastMRI), heart (CMRxRecon2023) and carotid (in-house), LoopMR significantly outperforms E2E-VarNet, PromptMR and PromptMR+ in PSNR and SSIM at every acceleration factor (p < 0.01), with about 1/9 of PromptMR+'s parameters (10.3M versus 92.9M). It also keeps its lead at unseen acceleration factors and on an unseen dataset. With our transformer block, the shared model matches or outperforms its distinct-weight counterpart at 6, 12 and 24 iterations. At a fixed number of iterations, shared transformer blocks match or outperform their distinct-weight versions, while shared CNN blocks perform worse. These results suggest that looping one well-chosen block can outperform stacking distinct cascades in MRI reconstruction, with a fraction of the parameters.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Adapting Monocular Depth Estimation in Novel Scenes through Disparity Refinement and Robot Ego-Motion
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: The geometric understanding of a scene is a crucial component for safe and efficient robotic operations in novel and unstructured environments. The recent emergence of foundation models for Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) has provided an opportunity to enrich robotic perception capabilities with dense long-range depth predictions, replacing expensive onboard hardware (e.g., LiDARs and stereo cameras). However, these offline models are primarily trained on affine-invariant depth representations, and their generalization to novel scenes remains unclear. In this work we present EM-ViT, a monocular depth estimation model that learns to adapt online relative depth inputs from a foundation model prior to the metric scale with observations collected during robotic operations. Motivated by the stereo camera parameterization, our method decomposes depth prediction via dense disparity refinement to recover the scene's relative structure and an effective baseline scalar prediction to determine the missing metric scale. The learning process leverages sparse LiDAR points and, optionally, the robot's Ego-Motion (EM) to rapidly train a lightweight Vision Transformer (ViT), while an internal gradient matching loss preserves the fine-grained semantic structure of the input disparity in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on publicly available sequences, such as KITTI, and show that our online learning pipeline can adapt to novel scenes faster and with higher accuracy than existing MDE foundation models. The code and supplementary materials will be publicly available at https://emvit-mde.github.io.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Poison-then-Hide: Finetuning-Activated Backdoor Attack on Pretrained Vision Encoders
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Backdoor attacks threaten the integrity of machine learning models by allowing attackers to control model behavior through triggers. Models can be compromised during finetuning by backdoor attacks through either poisoned data or adversarial training objectives. Because existing finetuning-activated attacks assume limited domain shift or frozen encoder layers, they often fail under full-model finetuning. We target a stealthy finetuning-activated attack where a dormant backdoor is implanted in a pretrained encoder, and later activated by finetuning on clean downstream data. We propose Poison-then-Hide, a novel attack that remains effective when the entire model is finetuned in a domain transfer. Our approach consists of three components: trigger optimization, base encoder poisoning, and targeted unlearning to conceal the backdoor. We evaluate our method on six datasets and three model architectures, and achieve state-of-the-art (up to 97%) attack success rates. We find that jointly learning the benign target task alongside the poisoning is critical to the attack's success. We demonstrate standard detection and mitigation defenses cannot fully remove the backdoor, which can reappear after benign finetuning.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Aggregate Accuracy Hides Diagnosis-Specific Failure in Medical Vision-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) are compared mainly by accuracy averaged across findings, a summary that can hide complete failure on a single diagnosis. We audit five open medical VLMs (MedGemma-4B, Lingshu-7B, HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and MedVLM-R1) on 6,048 ChestX-ray14 questions balanced by sex, age, finding, and label. On the 432 pneumothorax-positive X-rays, HuatuoGPT-Vision and Qwen2.5-VL detect zero cases while MedGemma and Lingshu detect 38% and 67% of the same images. The two failing models answer "no" to all 864 pneumothorax cases (balanced accuracy 0.500, chance), yet produce fluent, anatomically specific explanations that name the signs of a collapsed lung and then deny them, with no hedge or abstention. This failure is not an artifact of prompting, image resolution, label ambiguity, or model scale. It persists across four prompt formats, at native resolution, and on single-label cases. A within-model control shows the same forced prompt gives HuatuoGPT 79% recall on nodule but only 6% on pneumothorax. It survives a tenfold scale increase (Qwen2.5-VL-72B detects 4%) and replicates on SIIM-ACR, an independent dataset with radiologist-drawn masks, where the failing models detect 0 of 432 confirmed pneumothoraces, including 0 of the 144 largest lesions. Reading the models' logits and internal states shows this is not blindness. The two failing models are highly confident yet no better than chance and a linear probe recovers pneumothorax from their hidden representations even where recall is zero, so the finding is represented internally but suppressed at the output. Aggregate accuracy therefore cannot establish that a medical VLM can see a given finding, because a model that misses one can still describe it convincingly. Reporting per-finding recall and specificity on balanced cases is needed to tell the difference.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Coarse-to-Fine 3D MRI Reconstruction via Resolution-Agnostic Neural Operators
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Deep-learning-based 3D MRI reconstruction is limited in practice by the GPU memory and compute cost of full-volume training; 3D acquisitions are thus most often reconstructed by 2D models applied slice-by-slice and then stacked, which ignores through-plane (stacking-axis) structure. We reconstruct in full 3D and ask whether a model can be trained at low resolution (fast and memory-feasible) yet deployed at higher resolution. This coarse-to-fine strategy needs reliable cross-resolution performance, but standard networks are resolution-specific and degrade substantially when evaluated outside the training setting. We therefore use resolution-agnostic neural operators (NOs) and propose KIR-NO (k-space-to-Image Reconstruction Neural Operator), a discretization-agnostic framework for accelerated 3D MRI reconstruction. KIR-NO is trained with full backpropagation on low-resolution volumes and applied zero-shot to higher-resolution volumes at inference. Its core building block is a 3D neural operator based on discrete-continuous convolutions: convolutional filters are parameterized in a continuous basis and sampled at arbitrary voxel resolutions while preserving the local inductive bias of convolution. KIR-NO integrates these learned operators with physics-based consistency: a k-space neural-operator head first refines the undersampled Fourier measurements, and image-space neural-operator cascades then refine the reconstruction through interleaved data-consistency updates. Across 3D knee and brain MRI benchmarks, KIR-NO improves over classical and CNN baselines: it improves over a state-of-the-art 3D CNN by 2.2 dB PSNR at half resolution under 4x acceleration on SKM-TEA, with gains persisting at 8x and 16x. These results show that resolution-agnostic operators make coarse-to-fine 3D MRI reconstruction - cheap low-resolution training with high-resolution deployment - practical across anatomies.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: AROMA: Adaptive Representation-Oriented Multimodal Actuation for Vision-Language Model Control
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Mechanistic localization does not by itself yield usable control: causal sensitivity may occupy little activation energy, an accurate local direction may fail at finite scale, and a reachable numeral target may be wrong. We introduce AROMA (Adaptive Representation-Oriented Multimodal Actuation), a frozen-VLM control framework separating where to intervene, which geometry and gain to use, how to reach a target, which target to pursue, and when to act. In Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct, four dimensions of a causally validated cross-attention head explain 89.82% of cardinality sensitivity but only 9.52% of median activation energy; magnitude-normalized causal subspace actuation converts this mismatch into finite control, improving exact-count accuracy on untouched procedural data by +8.00 pp. Iterative Minimal-Effort Actuation (MEA) reaches 81.25% of oracle targets versus 15.18% for a frozen direction under matched step budgets. With target and gate frozen before evaluation, targeted MEA improves the previous frozen policy from 34.444% to 38.730% on a new natural Stage-2 cohort (N=630; paired p=4.63e-7) and yields 65.741% versus 65.153% over all 7,992 examples while editing only 63 inputs. Prospective routing, replication across heads and models, and comparisons with attribution-steering baselines further characterize each stage, separating localization, actuation, reachability, target quality, and selective deployment as distinct control problems.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Are We Ready for Snow-tonomous Driving? Challenges Toward Robust Automated Driving in Extreme Weather
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary:
Automated driving has gained remarkable momentum over the past decade, with both industry and academia investing substantial resources in developing perception and control solutions to advance vehicle autonomy. However, these efforts have largely focused on clear-weather scenarios, leaving harsh conditions, such as snow, rain, and fog, comparatively understudied. As a result, inclement weather remains one of the most significant hurdles for autonomous vehicles, often leading to substantial performance degradation in downstream perception and control tasks.
  In this paper, we present insights from the EU-funded Horizon Europe project ROADVIEW, which aims to develop robust, weather-aware perception and control modules for connected and automated vehicles operating under severe conditions, including snow, rain, and fog. Drawing on four years of large-scale development and real-world demonstrations across multiple vehicle platforms in different locations, we identify ten key challenges that hinder the development of weather-resilient autonomy, including data scarcity, domain shifts, limitations in multimodal perception, control robustness, and validation gaps, among others. We summarize these challenges and lessons learned toward enabling reliable snow-autonomous driving, highlighting critical directions for future research and standardization.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Supervision-Aware Evaluation of MedGemma for Reference-Assisted Radiotherapy Contour Ranking
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Radiotherapy contour ranking can support quality assurance, but vision-language model (VLM) gains may reflect supervision, score construction, available inputs, or representation access. We evaluated frozen MedGemma 1.5 in a single-institution study, a 12-patient held-out HaN-Seg test, five-fold cross-fitting on 30 non-test HaN-Seg patients, and transfer without refitting to 120 SegRap2023 patients. On held-out HaN-Seg, a supervised readout of the final prompt state exceeded a supervised readout of the model's yes/no output probabilities by +0.3047 pooled average precision (AP; 95% patient-bootstrap interval [+0.2822, +0.3269]); the advantage persisted against a parameter-count-matched nonlinear control. A readout of projected visual tokens exceeded the final-state readout in cross-fitting and transfer (+0.0706 AP averaged equally across patients on SegRap; 95% interval [+0.0607, +0.0804]), while a structured panel-feature readout remained competitive with visual tokens. The anatomy-conditioned readout did not demonstrate an advantage over the native-feature comparator. These results motivate visual-token and structured-feature controls in medical-imaging VLM evaluations; outcomes were computational or synthetic, not clinical acceptability.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SkillEarth: Teaching General-Purpose Agents to Act on Earth via Skill Evolution
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recently developed remote sensing (RS) agents execute real-world tasks with complex workflows through multi-step tool invocation. These agents, however, typically rely on predefined expertise or parameter updates. They thus require updating expert knowledge or retraining models whenever new tools, tasks, or execution patterns emerge, limiting their continual adaptability in dynamic Earth environments. In this work, we seek to equip general-purpose agents with RS tool-call knowledge that can be automatically extracted from demonstrated trajectories without expert intervention or parameter updates. Specifically, we propose SkillEarth, a self-evolving skill extraction method that externalizes RS tool-call knowledge as reusable, retrievable, and evolvable skill files and refines them through observation-grounded evolution. Unlike existing automatic skill extraction methods that rely on outcome-based reflection to refine skills holistically, SkillEarth grounds skill evolution in real tool-chain execution and combines dual-judge feedback with a grounded observation routing graph for precise component-level refinement. The resulting skills are generalizable, reliable, and transferable: they improve overall RS tool-call performance across three frontier LLMs and four open-source LLMs, are refined through real tool execution feedback, and support cross-model reuse without retraining. Experiments on OpenEarth-Bench and Earth-Bench demonstrate that SkillEarth achieves better tool selection, argument correctness, execution-order consistency, and task completion than existing RS agents and skill extraction methods.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: What Makes a VLA Reactive? A Study of Execution Strategies for Dynamic Manipulation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, and when objects move, those chunks go stale before they are executed. We study what makes a pretrained VLA reactive, using \pihalf{} on two dynamic simulation benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. We vary the prediction and execution horizons, compare synchronous and asynchronous inference, test methods that deliver actions sooner or keep successive chunks continuous, and adapt the policy with motion cues and latent-space reinforcement learning. The best prediction horizon is about one second, and the best execution horizon depends on the checkpoint. Short horizons help more with asynchronous execution, and methods that keep the trajectory continuous outperform those that only reduce latency. Adapting the policy repairs targeted failures, but on the conveyor task changing the execution horizon gained as much. Reactivity depends on the execution pipeline as much as on the policy, so both should be evaluated together.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Reading the Table: Sim-to-Real Game State Detection for the Chef's Hat Card Game
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Tabletop games offer a compelling scenario to study the interaction between artificial and human agents, combining social interaction with game state tracking and physical manipulation. To assess the game state, a robot needs to precisely detect closely related game objects, such as different card designs, requiring dedicated training data that is costly to annotate in the real world. Instead, we develop a fully automated synthetic data collection pipeline, using re-projection of known 3D coordinates to generate labels automatically and domain randomization to bridge the reality gap. This approach is used to collect a dataset of 25413 samples to finetune an object detection and a segmentation model, which are combined to assign detected cards to game-relevant zones and infer the game state. When evaluated on a real NICO humanoid robot, our pipeline achieves an F1-score of 0.906 for card-to-zone assignment, thus providing the perceptual foundation for a robot that can autonomously play Chef's Hat against human players.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: EMS-Nav: Embodied Multi-Scale Navigation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Industrial inspection robots must reach work areas and specific equipment. These destinations span spatial scales from regions to objects, so robots must relate each target to its surroundings to interpret the task and determine where to go. Existing methods support multi-scale navigation through rich environment representations, but at substantial computational and storage cost. These costs limit deployment where wireless coverage is incomplete and robots must rely on onboard computation to keep navigating. We introduce EMS-Nav, a biologically inspired multi-scale navigation framework for online, on-device operation. Its core innovation is to organize perception, spatial understanding, and navigation around regions, making local spaces the basic units of both environmental understanding and computation. EMS-Nav groups objects and their relationships into functionally meaningful spaces and builds a hierarchy from local areas to the broader environment. This organization supports efficient map construction alongside the interpretation and execution of language goals at different scales. In multi-scale navigation experiments, EMS-Nav achieves the highest success rates across all four target categories: objects, rooms, regions, and specific instances. It outperforms state-of-the-art open-vocabulary mapping and navigation methods, improving overall first-attempt success by 9.39 percentage points over the strongest baseline while reducing mapping overhead and language-model input size. Local deployment in real indoor environments further demonstrates its applicability to on-device embodied navigation. By establishing regions as the organizing basis for perception, spatial understanding, and language-guided action, EMS-Nav provides a system that combines multi-scale understanding with computational efficiency to support diverse language goals on resource-constrained robots.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Physics-based simulation unlocks scaling laws for generalizable MRI reconstruction
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Deep-learning-based magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction holds great promise for accelerating acquisitions, yet its clinical translation remains bottlenecked by poor generalizability across unseen scanners, populations, anatomies, and protocols. Gathering sufficiently diverse clinical datasets to overcome this bottleneck is hindered by high acquisition costs, privacy restrictions, and institutional biases. Here, we introduce Scalable Inverse Model (SIM), a framework that systematically co-designs physics-simulated training data, model architecture, and learning paradigms around scalability--leveraging compute scaling to overcome historical data bottlenecks and achieve robust zero-shot MRI reconstruction. Across 14 public and in-house datasets--spanning seven international centers, five vendors, field strengths of 0.3-7 T, over ten anatomical regions, more than ten acquisition protocols, downstream quantitative and molecular tasks, and a 150-scan blinded radiologist study--SIM demonstrates robust zero-shot generalizability, recovering fine anatomical details while suppressing aliasing artifacts where conventional deep-learning methods fail. Attention-map analyses confirm that SIM learns physically explainable, dynamically adaptive reconstruction primitives rather than anatomy-specific priors. SIM establishes a scalable, privacy-preserving, and democratized infrastructure for universal MRI reconstruction, providing a blueprint for generalizable AI across inverse problems in medical imaging.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MOSAIC: Modular Obstacle and Spatial-Aware Framework for Manipulation In Cluttered Scenes
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in robotic manipulation, yet most rely primarily on 2D visual observations and language instructions, leaving scene geometry and obstacle relationships to be inferred implicitly. This limitation is particularly problematic in cluttered environments, where small spatial errors can lead to unintended contacts or collisions. We propose MOSAIC, a modular spatial- and obstacle-aware framework that can be integrated with pretrained VLA policies to improve object-level scene understanding and action generation. Our method augments the VLA backbone with an auxiliary semantic grounding task that predicts role-specific masks for the target object, destination region, and surrounding obstacles. We further combine the target and destination masks with depth estimated from 3D scene reconstruction to construct role-specific geometric tokens that are injected directly into the action expert. In addition, we propose obstacle-aware attention supervision that emphasizes obstacles near the robot body during task execution. The resulting attention features are subsequently injected into later action-expert layers to further guide action generation. Together, these components provide explicit semantic, geometric, and obstacle-aware cues while preserving the underlying pretrained VLA architecture. We evaluate our framework on pretrained VLA model using the RoboPRO benchmark, including visual perturbation tests, and further validate it on real-world manipulation tasks. MOSAIC improves the success rate by 5.1% in cluttered scenes, and by 9.7% under visual perturbations, with gains of up to 25.0% in the most challenging environment. We will release our code and dataset upon acceptance at the following Github page: https://mmahdavian.github.io/MOSAIC/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: I See What You Want: Decoding Hierarchical Operator Intent from Visual Teleoperation History
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a powerful foundation for robotic scene understanding, task planning, and language-conditioned control. A natural question follows: can these models also decode what a human operator intends while teleoperating a robot, without any explicit instruction? We formulate this as hierarchical intent prediction, jointly inferring the ongoing atomic action and the broader mission it serves from a short visual teleoperation history. To study this, we introduce VI AMO (Vision Intention Action and Mission Ongoing), a dataset of 6,600 episodes from eleven robot sources with 13,653 temporally aligned action annotations and 9,702 mission annotations. Large proprietary models struggle with this problem: on held-out episodes, GPT-4o reaches Sentence-BERT similarities of only 0.563 and 0.470 for action and mission, and GPT-5.6 Luna achieves only 0.581 and 0.554. Fine-tuning a VLM on VI AMO yields our Vision-Intention Model (VIM), which raises these scores to 0.825 and 0.821 and still reaches 0.726 and 0.717 on the 35.4% of test actions with both labels absent from training. Finally, as a downstream application, VIM's predicted mission enables a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to take over from the operator mid-task in a real-world environment unseen during VIM fine-tuning, reducing human teleoperation time by 34.6% relative to GPT-4o and 39.8% relative to GPT-5.6 Luna, while cutting intent-prediction latency by roughly 70% on average.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: From State of THE ART to Human Prediction Algorithms
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Human curiosity and longing for the future have driven human progress from ancient times to the present. With the advancement of AI technology, human prediction algorithms have also drawn increasing attention from researchers. However, as AI technology continues to advance, we observe a counterintuitive phenomenon. Take human trajectory prediction algorithms as an example. Although models' quantitative prediction performance has improved, yielding one state-of-the-art model after another, the consideration of human behaviors, future thoughts, and social interactions themselves presents a gradually diminishing trend in the construction of these prediction algorithms, buried beneath numbers and metrics. In this manuscript, taking interactive art and human trajectory prediction algorithms as examples, we attempt to adopt a different analytical perspective to analyze the structural and developmental commonalities between these two fields. By examining specific interactive artworks and prediction algorithms, we aim to explore how human intuitions and art are associated with AI algorithms through three aspects, including perception, interaction, and timing, thereby providing new insights for the understanding and further research in this domain. We also observe an interesting phenomenon that certain art-inspired prediction algorithms can actually deduce intriguing patterns of human behaviors from the data, offering new potential avenues for understanding the relationship between human activities, state of The Art, and AI algorithms.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Safety as a Budget: Calibrating the Control Channel of Constrained GRPO for Vision-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Reinforcement learning can teach vision-language models (VLMs) to decline harmful image-text requests, but how safe the result becomes is set indirectly, through reward weights found by trial runs. Stating safety as budgets on the rate of harmful assistance and the rate of over-refusal, enforced by Lagrange multipliers inside GRPO with an off-the-shelf scorer as the cost, is the natural fix, and it fails twice. The multiplier compares the scorer's mean with the budget, and scorers built for ranking get the mean wrong: a fixed-point analysis shows that the mean bias, not the budget, then decides whether the multiplier settles, saturates or switches off. And standard GRPO standardizes the penalized reward within each group, which cancels the multiplier before it reaches the gradient. Two-channel constrained GRPO repairs both: the base reward keeps the raw score for the within-group comparison, the penalty and the constraint estimate pass through a monotone map fitted on judge-labeled training responses, and the advantage keeps the multiplier. On a Qwen3-VL-2B policy with a training-free readout of an open 4B model as the scorer, held-out harm on 1,037 adversarial prompts falls from 8.9% under standard GRPO to 4.8%, lower in every seed, where the uncalibrated budget gives 7.6%; over-refusal stays at most 2% on 400 benign queries and MMBench is unchanged. The gain is largest where the intent sits in the image (10.1% -> 5.1%) and grows on the unseen HADES benchmark (28.9% -> 12.8%). Order-preserving distortions of the scores reproduce each predicted controller state in every seed, and the results hold under a map fitted on another judge's labels, an image-reading judge and a human audit.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Asymmetric Multimodal Learning with Decomposed JEPAs
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary:
Cross-modal alignment is the standard objective for building multimodal representations. We show that alignment as a \emph{sole} objective is lossy wherever modalities are informationally asymmetric---where neither can express what the other carries. Visual question answering is an obvious case: a question is a selective relational operator probing a dense visual field whose fine-grained features no query recovers, so what alignment preserves is not what the task requires. We prove an \textbf{Alignment Redundancy Bound}: alignment-only Dirichlet energy minimization retains at most the redundant information atom $\Red(Z; X_1, X_2)$, annihilating private modality-specific structure $\Unq(Z; X_m)$ and cross-modal synergy $\Syn(Z; X_1, X_2)$.
  We introduce \textbf{Decomposed JEPA (D-JEPA)}, which factorizes latents into an aligned shared core and private modality-specific fibers. The shared core retains most of the structure alignment targets; the private fibers recover what alignment discards, via contextual masked prediction and asymmetric cross-subspace independence. Under information asymmetry, alignment-only training undergoes catastrophic semantic collapse on compositional reasoning benchmarks, surviving only on binary queries. D-JEPA averts this collapse, substantially improving downstream accuracy over both alignment-only and alignment-with-reconstruction baselines, and restoring a positive multimodal synergy gap in place of the baseline's inverted gap. Information-theoretic audits confirm that D-JEPA recovers most of the mutual information available from a frozen backbone, and causal fiber-swap interventions demonstrate that the recovered information is causally localized in the private fibers.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Dataset Distillation via Drifting
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: The task of dataset distillation concerns the learning of a small set of synthetic samples that can serve as an effective replacement for a large real dataset when used for downstream tasks. While many solutions have been proposed since the problem's inception, most of them primarily seek to optimize the distilled data with respect to a classifier. In this work, we propose a new distillation method that learns a set of samples such that they directly approximate the per-class data distribution. Specifically, we "drift" our distilled data in the latent space of a feature extractor such that they move both toward the real data and away from each other without using a classification objective. We find that our drifted data cover the real distribution significantly better than existing methods while still serving as powerful training samples for classification. Furthermore, we showcase our method's use as a visualization tool for better interpreting models and extend it beyond images to other modalities. Our work advances the frontier of dataset distillation, offering a novel synthesis method and proposing distribution-based metrics as a complementary evaluation. More broadly, our findings help address the growing need to understand both data and models by uncovering more about how they interact.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: AgriSense: Vision-Language Decision Support and Robotic Intervention in a Virtual Greenhouse Copy title
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Autonomous greenhouse management increasingly requires robotic systems that integrate perception, navigation, environmental regulation, and plant-level intervention. This paper presents AgriSense, a framework combining an Isaac Sim virtual greenhouse, a quadruped mobile manipulator, RGB and LiDAR-inertial sensing, environmental control, and supervised vision-language decision support. Frozen DINOv2 and BERT encoders, together with structured environmental inputs, support joint prediction of twelve environmental references, a target zone, and an intervention flag. Checkpoint replay reproduces 41/43 zone decisions. Across five seeds on a source-grouped test set, the full, image-removed, and language-removed configurations each achieve 43/44 correct zone decisions, providing no evidence of incremental multimodal zone-accuracy improvement. The full model achieves mean absolute errors of 0.249 degrees C for temperature, 2.030 percentage points for humidity, and 0.997 percentage points for soil moisture. Sensor-only inputs match full-model zone accuracy, while language-only inputs achieve 68.64%. External real-image benchmarks reveal distribution-shift limitations. Five offline Point-LIO routes yield rigidly aligned trajectory errors of 5.22-17.32 mm. Of 40 virtual-arm targets, 32 satisfy geometric acceptance criteria and eight are rejected at boundaries. Six long-horizon climate cases and fault protocols characterize integration limits. Navigation and integrated treatment rely on simulator-state inputs; physical greenhouse performance and agronomic treatment efficacy remain unvalidated. The contribution is an evaluated decision-support and robotic-intervention framework for a virtual greenhouse.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Spatiotemporal learning improves quantification of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Pore-space evolution and fluid displacement influence how rocks transmit and store fluids, affecting geological carbon storage, underground hydrogen storage and groundwater contaminant transport. A single time-resolved micro-CT experiment may produce tens to hundreds of three-dimensional images, and segmentation is required to quantify physical properties and run image-based simulations. Traditional methods such as thresholding perform poorly on noisy, low-contrast images and need manual adjustment per image; 3D deep learning networks segment each image without temporal information, so their errors vary between images and could be mistaken for physical change. Here we introduce a transformer-based 4D segmentation framework combining spatial and temporal information. It uses sequential images to resolve ambiguous phase assignments and separate physical change from segmentation error. The method is tested on images of mineral dissolution: it measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries more accurately than an equivalent 3D model that ignores temporal information. It also captures the increase in permeability verified against reference segmentations and flow simulations. The advantage transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining. On two other datasets of fluid displacement, it reduces spurious changes in predicted rock and porosity fluctuations and accurately identifies filling events. Spatiotemporal segmentation turns sequences of hundreds of three-dimensional images into more reliable quantitative measurements of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement without per-image parameter adjustment to support the analysis of time-resolved CT imaging.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: UAV-Flow++: A Unified Suite for Benchmarking and Learning Language-Guided UAV Flight
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Language-guided UAV navigation has largely focused on long-horizon route planning, leaving short-range, object-relative flight maneuvers underexplored. To address this gap, we formulate Flying-on-a-Word (Flow), a task requiring a UAV to convert concise natural-language instruction, egocentric visual observation, and current state dynamics into continuous flight actions. Flow encompasses both primitive motion commands and complex object-interactive behaviors, assessing motion intent comprehension and spatial context grounding. To enable policy learning and closed-loop evaluation, we introduce UAV-Flow, a comprehensive dataset comprising 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories across eight distinct motion categories, alongside 10,109 simulation trajectories in the UAV-Flow-Sim environment equipped with task-specific completion criteria. Furthermore, we develop FlowVLA, which undergoes imitation pretraining on mixed real-sim demonstrations and online post-training via Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). By leveraging group reward distributions, TGRPO effectively reinforces high-reward action sequences. Evaluated on 273 held-out UAV-Flow-Sim episodes, pretrained FlowVLA achieves a mean success rate of 75.58%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.72 percentage points, which TGRPO post-training further elevates to 93.16% with superior sample efficiency. Physical UAV experiments demonstrate robust execution of object-relative commands in both indoor and outdoor real-world scenes. Together, Flow establishes a novel benchmark and learning framework for language-conditioned flight maneuvers.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Neural Render Proxies for Interactive and Differentiable Lighting
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Within the CG animation production pipeline, the challenges artists tackle in Lighting can be immense. Even minor adjustments require re-rendering massive scenes with slow offline renderers; global illumination has to be sampled and complex shaders have to be evaluated, leading to iteration times of minutes to hours per frame. To accelerate this process, we introduce a novel neural render proxy (NRP) that enables differentiable relighting of static scenes with fixed camera and materials at interactive rates. Our main insight is the decoupling of traditional rendering into path sampling and emission computation. From a single, light-agnostic render pass, we collect light transport data in the form of path samples. This enables rapidly sampling lighting conditions on the fly, and training a scene-specific lightweight neural network that learns how light is transported from any scene location to any image pixel. This approach is compatible with non-differentiable production renderers, induces minimal memory requirements during inference, and scales only with resolution and the number of light sources and parameters, but independently of scene and appearance complexity. Our evaluation demonstrates interactive frame rates for relighting (~30-60 Hz) while closely approximating the visual fidelity of ground-truth path tracing. In addition, the differentiable NRP enables fast, gradient-based inverse workflows, allowing artists to efficiently solve for lighting parameters from intuitive image-space edits or generative targets.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ProtoVis-Nav: Prototypical Visual Imagination for Visual-Spatial Aligned UAV Navigation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision language navigation (VLN) is very challenging for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) since small errors in 3D motion prediction can lead to navigation errors and collisions. Unable to fathom execution outcomes in 3D environments, existing methods often struggle to predict accurate navigation waypoints from language instructions. To solve this, we introduce the Prototypical Visual Imagination framework, shortened as ProtoVis-Nav, which forces the model to imagine an outcome-associated local visual representation for the intended next UAV movement. Specifically, we predict feature prototypes and use their linear combination to estimate the visual feature of the target region. In this manner, the VLN model first imagines the local visual representation of the next intended location, and then uses predicted prototypes as context for generating the final action, promoting alignment between visual context and waypoint outputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the ProtoVis-Nav framework and show substantial improvements over existing baselines.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Contrastive Semi-Supervised Segmentation with Class-wise Patches and Silhouette-Adaptive Consistency
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We present CSSL, a contrastive semi-supervised method for medical image segmentation. CSSL samples class-wise patches from labelled images and from confident pseudo-labels, separates their embeddings with a supervised contrastive loss with mixed hard negatives, and uses the Silhouette coefficient of the embedding clusters to set the strength of a feature-perturbation consistency loss. On MoNuSeg, patch embeddings are obtained by masked pooling of the encoder features of the unmasked image, nucleus rims form an additional contrastive class and a memory bank stores past embeddings; on CHAOS, patches are pixel-masked and no memory bank is used. The CSSL losses are added to a weak-to-strong pseudo-labelling recipe. We follow the protocols of published baselines: Self-Loop on MoNuSeg and DAFNet on CHAOS. On MoNuSeg with 50% labels, CSSL reaches 80.87 $\pm$ 0.17 nuclei F1 over three label splits, compared with 79.10 for Self-Loop and 78.73 for the same recipe without CSSL. On CHAOS T2 with 25% labels, CSSL reaches 89.01 Dice, compared with 82.0 for DAFNet and 88.94 for the recipe alone. Ablations show that the contrastive branch and, on MoNuSeg, the boundary class and feature-level pooling account for most of the improvement. Code: https://github.com/prinshul/CSSL

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Explainable Classifier for Malignant Lymphoma Subtyping via Cell Graph and Image Fusion
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Lymphoma subtype classification has a direct impact on treatment and outcomes, necessitating models that are both accurate and explainable. This study proposes a novel explainable Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) framework that identifies subtype-specific Regions of Interest (ROIs) from Whole Slide Images (WSIs) while integrating features of cell distribution and image. Our framework simultaneously addresses three objectives: (1) indicating appropriate ROIs for each subtype, (2) explaining the frequency and spatial distribution of characteristic cell types, and (3) reaching accurate subtyping using both cell distribution and image modalities. Our method fuses cell graph and image features extracted for each patch in a WSI by a Mixture-of-Experts-based approach and classifies subtypes within an MIL framework. Experiments on a dataset of 1,233 WSIs demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy compared to ten other methods and provides region- and cell-level explanations that align with a pathologist's perspective.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention - MICCAI 2025, LNCS 15971, pp. 320-330

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Fractal-Informed Spatial-Frequency Adaptation for Texture Generation in Natural Image Compression
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Generative image compression aims to reconstruct realistic images at low bitrates by balancing the trade-off among rate, distortion, and realism. However, recovering plausible textures while preserving reconstruction fidelity remains challenging, particularly under limited bandwidth. In this paper, we propose a diffusion-informed generative image compression framework that exploits frequency-domain representations and diffusion knowledge to improve texture reconstruction. Specifically, we approach the rate-distortion-realism trade-off from three complementary perspectives. First, motivated by the close relationship between image textures and frequency characteristics, we develop a Fractal Frequency-Aware Band Image Compression (FFAB-IC) network to capture directional frequency components in natural images. By integrating fractal band operations into nonlinear neural transformations, the network preserves essential image information while suppressing redundant details. Second, we incorporate diffusion knowledge into the encoder and introduce iterative diffusion refinement into the decoder, enabling the recovery of realistic textures under constrained bitrates. Third, we introduce frequency- and content-aware regularization to jointly exploit spatial structures and frequency characteristics during optimization. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our method achieves a superior rate-distortion-realism trade-off, delivering higher realism at comparable distortion than existing approaches.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: LLM-to-Phy3D: Physically Conform Online 3D Object Generation with LLMs
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) has revolutionized the landscape of digital content creation in different modalities. However, its potential use in Physical AI for engineering design, where the production of physically viable artifacts is paramount, remains vastly underexplored. The absence of physical knowledge in existing LLM-to-3D models often results in outputs detached from real-world physical constraints. To address this gap, we introduce LLM-to-Phy3D, a physically conform online 3D object generation that enables existing LLM-to-3D models to produce physically conforming 3D objects on the fly. LLM-to-Phy3D introduces a novel online black-box refinement loop that empowers large language models (LLMs) through synergistic visual and physics-based evaluations. By delivering directional feedback in an iterative refinement process, LLM-to-Phy3D actively drives the discovery of prompts that yield 3D artifacts with enhanced physical performance and greater geometric novelty relative to reference objects, marking a substantial contribution to AI-driven generative design. Systematic evaluations of LLM-to-Phy3D, supported by ablation studies in vehicle design optimization, reveal various LLM improvements gained by 4.5% to 106.7% in producing physically conform target domain 3D designs over conventional LLM-to-3D models. The encouraging results suggest the potential general use of LLM-to-Phy3D in Physical AI for scientific and engineering applications.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: IEEE Congress on Evolutionary Computation (CEC) 2026

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PhysPatch: A Physically Realizable and Transferable Adversarial Patch Attack for Multimodal Large Language Models-based Autonomous Driving Systems
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are becoming integral to autonomous driving (AD) systems due to their strong vision-language reasoning capabilities. However, MLLMs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, particularly adversarial patch attacks, which can pose serious threats in real-world scenarios. Existing patch-based attack methods are primarily designed for object detection models and perform poorly when transferred to MLLM-based systems due to the latter's complex architectures and reasoning abilities. To address these limitations, we propose PhysPatch, a physically realizable and transferable adversarial patch framework tailored for MLLM-based AD systems. PhysPatch jointly optimizes patch location, shape, and content to enhance attack effectiveness and real-world applicability. It introduces a semantic-based mask initialization strategy for realistic placement, an SVD-based local alignment loss with patch-guided crop-resize to improve transferability, and a potential field-based mask refinement method. Extensive experiments across open-source, commercial, and reasoning-capable MLLMs demonstrate that PhysPatch significantly outperforms prior methods in steering MLLM-based AD systems toward target-aligned perception and planning outputs. Moreover, PhysPatch consistently places adversarial patches in physically feasible regions of AD scenes, ensuring strong real-world applicability and deployability.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Design, Implementation and Evaluation of a Real-Time Remote Photoplethysmography (rPPG) Acquisition System for Non-Invasive Vital Sign Monitoring
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: The growing integration of smart environments and low-power computing devices, coupled with mass-market sensor technologies, is driving advancements in remote and non-contact-based physiological monitoring. However, deploying these systems in real-time on resource-constrained platforms introduces significant challenges related to scalability, interoperability, and performance. This paper presents a computationally efficient real-time remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) system, designed to extract physiological signals, such as heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation (SpO2), from facial video streams. The system is built on the Face2PPG pipeline, which processes video frames sequentially for rPPG signal extraction and analysis, while leveraging a multithreaded architecture to manage video capture, real-time processing, network communication, and graphical user interface updates concurrently. This design targets continuous operation at 30 frames per second (FPS), with adaptive feedback through a collaborative user interface to guide optimal signal capture conditions. The network interface includes both an HTTP server for continuous video streaming and a RESTful API for on-demand vital sign retrieval. To ensure accurate performance despite limited computational resources, we use a hybrid programming model combining Functional Reactive Programming (FRP) and the Actor Model, allowing event-driven processing and efficient task parallelization. We evaluate HR accuracy on three public datasets (COHFACE, LGI-PPGI, and UBFC-RPPG), and conduct preliminary evaluations of RR on COHFACE and SpO2 on PURE. We also assess the processing time and end-to-end operation of the system on two computers, including live HR and SpO2 agreement with a medical-grade fingertip pulse oximeter across five 10-minute sessions. Our work addresses key challenges in real-time contactless biosignal monitoring.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MedGS: Gaussian Splatting for Multi-Modal 3D Medical Imaging
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multi-modal three-dimensional (3D) medical imaging data, derived from ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and computed tomography (CT), provide a widely adopted approach for non-invasive anatomical visualization. However, accurate modeling depends on surface reconstruction and frame-to-frame interpolation, where traditional methods often struggle with image noise and incomplete information between sparse frames. To address these challenges, we present \our{}, a novel framework based on Gaussian Splatting (GS) designed for high-fidelity 3D anatomical reconstruction. Uniquely, \our{} employs a multi-task architecture that simultaneously performs frame interpolation and segmentation using a unified geometric representation. By coupling these tasks, the model leverages dense signals from image synthesis to regularize the geometry, enabling high-quality surface extraction even from a limited number of input frames. Specifically, medical data are modeled as Folded-Gaussians with dual color attributes, supported by an In-Between Frame Regularization (IBFR) mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that \our{} achieves higher metric scores than implicit neural representations and improves interpolation quality. Repository: https://github.com/gmum/MedGS

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: The SAGES Critical View of Safety Challenge: A Global Benchmark for AI-Assisted Surgical Quality Assessment
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) for surgical quality assessment promise to democratize access to expertise, with applications in training, guidance, and accreditation. This study presents the SAGES Critical View of Safety (CVS) Challenge, the first AI competition organized by a surgical society, using the CVS in laparoscopic cholecystectomy, a universally recommended yet inconsistently performed safety step, as an exemplar of surgical quality assessment. A global collaboration across 54 institutions in 24 countries engaged hundreds of clinicians and engineers to curate 1,000 videos annotated by 20 surgical experts according to a consensus-validated protocol. The challenge addressed key barriers to real-world deployment in surgery, including achieving high performance, capturing uncertainty in subjective assessment, and ensuring robustness to clinical variability. To enable this scale of effort, we developed EndoGlacier, a framework for managing large, heterogeneous surgical video and multi-annotator workflows. Thirteen international teams participated, achieving up to a 17% relative gain in assessment performance, over 62% reduction in calibration error, and a 17% relative improvement in robustness over the state-of-the-art. Analysis of results highlighted methodological trends linked to model performance, providing guidance for future research toward robust, clinically deployable AI for surgical quality assessment.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: How Diffusion Models Memorize
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Despite their success in image generation, diffusion models can unintentionally memorize and reproduce training data, raising serious privacy and copyright concerns. Although prior work has studied memorization from different perspectives, a unified account of how this reproduction occurs during generation remains incomplete. In this paper, we develop a mathematical account of this process in text-to-image latent diffusion models with classifier-free guidance. We trace reproduction across denoising steps through predictions of the final denoised latent made with and without the prompt. Assuming these predictions are Bayes-optimal and uniformly bounded, we show that sufficiently low loss on a training prompt--image pair enables the prediction made with the prompt to reproduce the paired training latent with high probability, even at the first denoising step. At this first step, we bound the difference between the prediction made without the prompt and the empirical mean of the training latents, showing how guidance amplifies the reproduced training latent's deviation from that mean. We then quantify how the latent passed between denoising steps carries prompt influence to subsequent predictions made without the prompt. When both predictions are sufficiently close to the paired training latent at the final step, their guided combination also reproduces it in the final generated latent. We also analyze how their difference evolves, showing that closer agreement alone does not establish reproduction. Finally, our account provides a unified explanation of existing detection and mitigation strategies.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Optimized Minimal 4D Gaussian Splatting for Efficient Dynamic Scene Representation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: 4D Gaussian Splatting has emerged as a new paradigm for dynamic scene representation, enabling real-time rendering of scenes with complex motions. However, it faces a major challenge of storage overhead, as millions of Gaussians are required for high-fidelity reconstruction. Compressing explicit 4D Gaussians is challenging because they exhibit heterogeneous redundancy across static and dynamic regions, and their temporal attributes make direct quantization unstable. In this work, we present OMG4 (Optimized Minimal 4D Gaussian Splatting), a framework that constructs a compact set of salient Gaussians capable of faithfully representing 4D Gaussian models. Our method progressively reduces Gaussians in three stages: (1) Gaussian Sampling to identify primitives critical to reconstruction fidelity, (2) Gaussian Pruning to remove redundancies, and (3) Gaussian Merging to fuse primitives with similar characteristics. In addition, we integrate implicit appearance compression and extend Sub-Vector Quantization (SVQ) to 4D representations with a staged quantization scheme, further reducing storage while preserving quality. Extensive experiments on standard benchmark datasets demonstrate that OMG4 achieves a favorable rate-distortion trade-off over recent state-of-the-art methods, reducing model sizes by over 60% while maintaining reconstruction quality. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of OMG4 as a practical framework for compact and high-fidelity 4D scene representation. Our source code is available at https://minshirley.github.io/OMG4/.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Robust Reasoning Segmentation for Open-World MLLMs without Catastrophic Forgetting
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Ensuring trustworthiness and versatility in Open-World Visual Recognition is a core goal of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While integrating segmentation is desirable, prevailing methods require invasive fine-tuning, which often leads to catastrophic forgetting of the model's general-purpose capabilities. This trade-off between task-specific performance and general reliability fundamentally undermines the goal of building unified, trustworthy systems. We introduce LENS (Leveraging kEypoiNts for MLLMs' Segmentation), a novel plug-and-play paradigm designed to equip MLLMs with pixel-level ability without compromising their foundational integrity. LENS attaches a lightweight head to a completely frozen MLLM, interpreting the intrinsic spatial cues embedded in attention maps. It extracts keypoints and translates them into prompt-compatible features for a mask decoder. Extensive experiments validate that LENS achieves segmentation performance competitive with retraining-based methods. Crucially, it largely preserves the MLLM's open-world generalization, avoiding the degradation observed in fine-tuned counterparts. By decoupling segmentation from generation, LENS offers a robust and efficient path toward truly multi-talented and reliable vision models.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: D2D: Detector-to-Differentiable Critic for Improved Numeracy in Text-to-Image Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have achieved strong performance in semantic alignment, yet they still struggle with generating the correct number of objects specified in prompts. Existing approaches typically incorporate auxiliary counting networks as external critics to enhance numeracy. However, since these critics must provide gradient guidance during generation, they are restricted to regression-based models that are inherently differentiable, thus excluding detector-based models with superior counting ability, whose count-via-enumeration nature is non-differentiable. To overcome this, we propose Detector-to-Differentiable (D2D), a novel framework that transforms non-differentiable detection models into differentiable critics, leveraging their superior counting ability to guide numeracy generation. Specifically, we design custom activation functions to convert detector logits into soft binary indicators, which are then used to optimize the noise prior at inference time with pre-trained T2I models. Our extensive experiments on SDXL-Turbo, SD-Turbo, and Pixart-DMD across four benchmarks of varying complexity (low-density, high-density, and multi-object scenarios) demonstrate consistent and substantial improvements in object counting accuracy (e.g., boosting up to 13.7% on D2D-Small, a 400-prompt, low-density benchmark), with minimal degradation in overall image quality and computational overhead. Project page: https://nobliney.github.io/d2d/.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Robust Image Emotion Classification via Multi-Level Affective Captioning
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Image emotion classification (IEC) has been studied for many years and has recently attracted increasing attention with the rapid development of deep learning. Although recent studies have benefited from knowledge embedded in pre-trained visual models, the performance is still limited by the "affective gap" between low-level visual features and high-level affective semantics. Psychological studies suggest that language can convey fine-grained and emotion-rich information. Inspired by this observation, we attempt to narrow the "affective gap" by introducing affective text. Specifically, we design a multi-level contrastive loss to detect emotional concepts from images and introduce an emotional-attribute-guided large language model approach to generate affective sentences. Then, a pre-trained language model is employed to combine emotional concepts with affective sentences for IEC. In addition, we introduce a contrastive loss with a semantic-similarity-based sampling strategy to address large intra-class differences and limited inter-class differences in affective datasets. Moreover, unlike many previous studies, we explicitly consider images containing embedded text. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that the proposed method helps narrow the "affective gap" and achieves competitive performance.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Towards Accurate UAV Image Perception: Guiding Vision-Language Models with Stronger Task Prompts
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: UAV image perception with VLMs aims to identify and localize targets based on semantic and spatial task prompts. However, small, densely distributed objects and cluttered backgrounds hinder these tasks, particularly when concise prompts provide insufficient guidance. Although task-specific fine-tuning improves image-text alignment, it requires large-scale annotations and model-specific updates, increasing adaptation costs across models and tasks. To address this, we propose AerialVP, a task-adaptive, training-free agent that adapts VLMs through prompt enhancement rather than parameter optimization. AerialVP dynamically adapts its enhancement strategy to the original prompt's specificity, selectively incorporating image-derived semantics, spatial positions, and object relationships. These cues provide discriminative descriptions and spatial constraints, leveraging VLMs' pretrained alignment and reasoning capabilities to improve image-text alignment and reduce target ambiguity. Specifically, an LLM-based Task Engine coordinates modular tools for prompt analysis, visual information extraction, and prompt fusion. The enhanced prompt and original image are then provided to the unchanged backend VLM for prediction. This prompt-centric strategy enables training-free adaptation across diverse open-source and proprietary VLMs. For systematic evaluation, we introduce AerialSense, a unified benchmark covering Aerial Visual Grounding, Aerial Visual Reasoning, and Aerial Visual Question Answering across diverse UAV scenes and imaging conditions. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across all three tasks and evaluated VLMs. AerialVP also achieves competitive performance against LoRA-based instruction fine-tuning, validating prompt-centric adaptation. Our work is available at https://github.com/lostwolves/AerialVP.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ReflFlow: Learning Geometry-Guided Ray Tracing for Dynamic Specular Reconstruction
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We present ReflFlow, a novel framework for high-fidelity rendering of dynamic specular scenes by addressing two key challenges: precise reflection direction estimation and physically accurate modeling. To achieve this, we propose a Residual Material-Augmented 2D Gaussian Splatting representation that models dynamic geometry and material properties, allowing accurate reflection ray computation. Furthermore, we introduce a Dynamic Environment Gaussian and a hybrid rendering pipeline that decomposes rendering into diffuse and specular components, enabling physically informed specular synthesis via rasterization and ray tracing. Finally, we devise a coarse-to-fine training strategy to improve optimization stability and promote physically meaningful decomposition. Extensive experiments on dynamic scene benchmarks demonstrate that ReflFlow outperforms prior methods quantitatively and qualitatively, producing sharper and more realistic specular reflections in complex dynamic environments.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306:119643-119658, 2026

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: GRCF: Group-wise Ranking and Calibration Framework for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Most multimodal sentiment analysis algorithms focus on point-wise regression. While straightforward, it uses absolute values to represent subjective sentiment and overlooks the ordinal nature of sentiment, resulting in unstable predictions and poor correlation. Inspired by the way humans perceive sentiment, pair-wise ordinal learning frameworks emerged to address this gap, capturing relative order by learning from comparisons. However, they have two limitations: First, they assign uniform importance to all pairs, failing to adaptively focus on hard-to-rank samples. Second, they employ static ranking margins, which fail to reflect the varying semantic distances between sentiment groups. To address this, we propose a Group-wise Ranking and Calibration Framework (GRCF) that introduces the Adaptive Error-weighting and Dynamic Margin mechanism, which resolves these limitations by simultaneously preserving the relative ordinal structure and ensuring absolute score calibration. Specifically, Stage 1 introduces a Group-aware Ranking Loss to build a fine-grained ordinal structure by assigning higher optimization priority to confusable pairs. Stage 2 then employs an MAE-driven objective to align the prediction magnitudes. To validate its generalizability, we extend GRCF to classification tasks, including Multimodal Humor and Sarcasm Detection. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on regression datasets while also showing strong generalizability in classification tasks.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Do Pathology Foundation Models Encode Disease Progression? A Pseudotime Analysis of Visual Representations
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision foundation models trained on discretely sampled images achieve strong performance on classification benchmarks, yet whether their representations encode the continuous processes underlying their training data remains unclear. This question is especially pertinent in computational pathology, where we posit that models whose latent representations implicitly capture ordinal disease progression may better reflect underlying biology, support more robust generalization, and enable quantitative analyses of features associated with disease transitions. Using diffusion pseudotime, a method developed to infer developmental trajectories from single-cell transcriptomics, we probe whether foundation models organize disease states along coherent progression directions in representation space. Across four cancer progressions and six models, we find that all pathology-specific models recover trajectory orderings significantly exceeding null baselines, with pathology vision-only models achieving the highest average fidelities. Model rankings by trajectory fidelity on reference diseases predict few-shot classification performance on held-out diseases ($\rho = 0.91$), and exploratory analysis shows cell-type composition varies along inferred trajectories in patterns consistent with known stromal remodeling. Together, these results suggest that vision foundation models can implicitly learn to represent continuous processes from independent static observations, and that trajectory fidelity provides a complementary measure of representation quality beyond downstream performance. While demonstrated in pathology, this framework could be applied to other domains where continuous processes are observed through static snapshots.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: VMonarch: Efficient Video Diffusion Transformers with Structured Attention
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: The quadratic complexity of the attention mechanism severely limits the context scalability of Video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). We find that the highly sparse spatio-temporal attention patterns exhibited in Video DiTs can be naturally represented by the Monarch matrix. It is a class of structured matrices with flexible sparsity, enabling sub-quadratic attention via an alternating minimization algorithm. Accordingly, we propose VMonarch, a novel attention mechanism for Video DiTs that enables efficient computation over the dynamic sparse patterns with structured Monarch matrices. First, we adapt spatio-temporal Monarch factorization to explicitly capture the intra-frame and inter-frame correlations of the video data. Second, we introduce a recomputation strategy to mitigate artifacts arising from instabilities during alternating minimization of Monarch matrices. Third, we propose a novel online entropy algorithm fused into FlashAttention, enabling fast Monarch matrix updates for long sequences. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VMonarch achieves comparable or superior generation quality to full attention on VBench after minimal tuning. It overcomes the attention bottleneck in Video DiTs, reduces attention FLOPs by a factor of 17.5, and achieves a speedup of over 5x in attention computation for long videos, surpassing state-of-the-art sparse attention methods at 90% sparsity. Code is available at https://github.com/EricLina/VMonarch.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: How Much of a Model Do We Need? Redundancy and Slimmability in Remote Sensing Foundation Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Large-scale foundation models (FMs) in remote sensing (RS) (denoted as RS FMs) are developed following paradigms established in computer vision (CV), yet the validity of transferring CV scaling laws to RS has not been systematically examined. We hypothesize that RS FMs enter an overparameterized regime at substantially smaller scales than their CV counterparts, with task-relevant information encoded redundantly across model dimensions. To test this hypothesis, we apply post-hoc slimmability, uniform width reduction of pretrained encoder transformer blocks, to measure representational redundancy across ten state-of-the-art RS FMs on classification, segmentation, and change detection. RS FMs retain on average over 85% relative accuracy on RS classification datasets under aggressive width reduction, while masked autoencoder (MAE) and DINOv2 pretrained on natural images (denoted as CV MAE and CV DINOv2) degrade sharply on ImageNet subsets of matched class count over the same range of computational requirements. A CV MAE evaluated directly on the same RS dataset narrows but does not close the gap, indicating that both dataset characteristics and domain-specific pretraining contribute to the differences between the models. Analyses of the representation space of the models indicate that task-relevant variance concentrates in few principal components and is redundantly encoded across model dimensions. We further show that learned slimmable training improves over post-hoc slimmability for contrastive objectives, but reconstruction-based objectives do not benefit consistently from current slimmable training protocols. Our findings establish post-hoc slimming as a practical deployment strategy for resource-constrained RS applications and as a diagnostic tool for representational redundancy in RS FMs. Code is available at https://github.com/hackelle/slimmable-remote-sensing-foundation-models.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MM-SCALE: Evaluating Evidence-Grounded Moral Judgment in Vision-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-Language Models increasingly make socially consequential judgments from image-text inputs, yet current evaluations often stop at verdict-level accuracy: whether the final label is human-aligned, not whether it follows from the correct evidence. We introduce MM-SCALE (Multimodal Moral SCALE), a benchmark for evidence-grounded moral judgment built around a design choice: each image is paired with multiple action scenarios, so models must compare how different actions interact with the same visual context rather than score images in isolation. MM-SCALE contains 8,444 image contexts and 21,977 action scenarios, each annotated with a 5-point moral acceptability rating and a modality-grounding label indicating whether the human judgment relied on text, image, or both. Three tasks evaluate whether models (i) assign calibrated scalar moral scores, (ii) preserve human orderings within a shared visual context, and (iii) ground rationales in the evidence source humans found critical to judgment. Across models, aggregate metrics overstate alignment: NDCG@5 remains high across models, while within-image pairwise accuracy remains only 0.53-0.62 even on scenario pairs whose human mean ratings differ by at least one point. CoT has inconsistent effects on calibration and does not reliably improve within-image ordering. Evidence grounding evaluations further show that models often describe visual context without making it critical for the verdict. These results reveal an evidence-grounding failure in current VLMs and position MM-SCALE as an evaluation testbed for moral judgment under shared image contexts. This dataset includes potentially harmful and sensitive visual content. Images are intended solely for evaluation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MMEarth-Bench: Global Model Adaptation via Multimodal Test-Time Training
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recent research in geospatial machine learning demonstrates that models pretrained with self-supervised learning on Earth observation data can perform well on downstream tasks with limited labeled data. However, most benchmark datasets have few data modalities and poor global representation, limiting the ability to evaluate multimodal pretrained models at global scales. In order to fill this gap, we introduce MMEarth-Bench, a collection of five new environmental tasks with 12 modalities, globally distributed data, and both random and geographic test splits. We benchmark a diverse set of pretrained models and find that while (multimodal) pretraining tends to improve model robustness in limited data settings, geographic generalization abilities remain poor. Moreover, a simple randomly initialized multimodal model is competitive given enough labeled data. Although data is abundant, models can currently only make use of the modalities on which they were pretrained. To solve this problem, we propose using all the modalities available at test time as auxiliary tasks for test-time adaptation. Our model-agnostic method for test-time training with multimodal reconstruction (TTT-MMR) can improve performance across all models and tasks on both test splits. Furthermore, geographic batching leads to a good trade-off between regularization and specialization during TTT, which can be beneficial for long-tail distributions. Our dataset, code, and visualization tool are linked on the project page.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Diff-Aid: Inference-time Adaptive Interaction Denoising for Rectified Text-to-Image Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recent text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have achieved remarkable advancement, yet faithfully following complex textual descriptions remains challenging due to insufficient interactions between textual and visual features. Prior approaches enhance such interactions via architectural design or handcrafted textual condition weighting, but lack flexibility and overlook the dynamic interactions across different blocks and denoising stages. To provide a more flexible and efficient solution to this problem, we propose Diff-Aid, a lightweight inference-time method that adaptively adjusts per-token text and image interactions across transformer blocks and denoising timesteps. Beyond improving generation quality, Diff-Aid yields interpretable modulation patterns that reveal how different blocks, timesteps, and textual tokens contribute to semantic alignment during denoising. As a plug-and-play module, Diff-Aid can be seamlessly integrated into downstream applications for further improvement, including style LoRAs, controllable generation, and zero-shot editing. Experiments on strong baselines (SD 3.5 and FLUX) demonstrate consistent improvements in prompt adherence, visual quality, and human preference across various metrics. Our code and models will be released.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MarsRetrieval: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Planetary-Scale Geospatial Retrieval on Mars
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Data-driven approaches like deep learning are rapidly advancing planetary science, particularly in Mars exploration. Despite recent progress, most existing benchmarks remain confined to closed-set supervised visual tasks and do not support text-guided retrieval for geospatial discovery. We introduce MarsRetrieval, a retrieval benchmark for evaluating vision-language models for Martian geospatial discovery. MarsRetrieval includes three tasks: (1) paired image-text retrieval, (2) landform retrieval, and (3) global geo-localization, covering multiple spatial scales and diverse geomorphic origins. We propose a unified retrieval-centric protocol to benchmark multimodal embedding architectures, including contrastive dual-tower encoders and generative vision-language models. Our evaluation shows MarsRetrieval is challenging: even strong foundation models often fail to capture domain-specific geomorphic distinctions. We further show that domain-specific fine-tuning is critical for generalizable geospatial discovery in planetary settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml-stat-Sustech/MarsRetrieval

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: VidEoMT: Your ViT is Secretly Also a Video Segmentation Model
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Existing online video segmentation models typically combine a per-frame segmenter with complex specialized tracking modules. While effective, these modules introduce significant architectural complexity and computational overhead. Recent studies suggest that plain Vision Transformer (ViT) encoders, when scaled with sufficient capacity and large-scale pre-training, can conduct accurate image segmentation without requiring specialized modules. Motivated by this observation, we propose the Video Encoder-only Mask Transformer (VidEoMT), a simple encoder-only video segmentation model that eliminates the need for dedicated tracking modules. To enable temporal modeling in an encoder-only ViT, VidEoMT introduces a lightweight query propagation mechanism that carries information across frames by reusing queries from the previous frame. To balance this with adaptability to new content, it employs a query fusion strategy that combines the propagated queries with a set of temporally-agnostic learned queries. As a result, VidEoMT attains the benefits of a tracker without added complexity, achieving competitive accuracy while being 5x-10x faster, running at up to 160 FPS with a ViT-L backbone. Code: https://github.com/tue-mps/videomt
